genZNote: The Candida species most at home on skin and catheters — it loves biofilms on central lines and IV fluids more than any other Candida species.

morphology.shape: Oval to elongated budding yeast; forms pseudohyphae, not true hyphae

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human skin and subungual spaces; also environmental surfaces
habitat.hostAssociation: Common skin commensal; opportunistic pathogen especially via intravascular devices
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Notable for surviving on hands and hospital surfaces and forming biofilms on plastic catheters and parenteral nutrition lines
habitat.reservoir: Human skin, healthcare workers' hands, indwelling catheters

microscopy.appearance: Budding yeast with pseudohyphae, no true hyphae

culture.growthCharacteristics: Grows well at 37°C, tolerates high glucose concentrations

identificationClues: Germ tube negative and lacks true hyphae, forming only pseudohyphae
Strong tendency to form biofilms on plastic medical devices (catheters, prosthetic material) and to grow well in glucose-rich IV fluids/parenteral nutrition
A leading cause of candidemia in neonatal intensive care units and in patients with central venous catheters
Frequently associated with healthcare workers' hands as a transmission source, unlike most endogenous Candida infections

diseases: Endocarditis (especially prosthetic valve, IV drug use)
virulenceFactors: Strong biofilm formation on plastic surfaces
clinicalImportance.transmission: Often exogenous — transmitted via contaminated hands, catheters, or IV fluids rather than purely endogenous overgrowth
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: One of the most common non-albicans Candida species in neonates and in patients with central venous catheters
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Catheter removal is often necessary for cure given its strong biofilm-forming tendency

examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Strongest biofilm-forming Candida species on plastic devices; classic neonatal ICU and catheter pathogen
